description: That pinch in the front of your hip when you squat deep is not a flexibility problem, and forcing stretches into it makes it worse. Run the hip rotation test, learn why the tissue at the front of your hip heals from mid-range load instead of compression, and get the one-week repair plan.

lines: Shin swings out, hip rotates in.
The stop point is the number.
beats.title: THE WIPER TEST

scenes.narration: Sit tall on the edge of a chair, both feet flat, knees bent at a right angle. Now keep one thigh completely still and let the shin swing outward like a windshield wiper, slowly, until it stops on its own. That stop point is your hip rotation. Pointing straight down is zero degrees. A full diagonal is forty five. Where your shin stops, somewhere between those two, is your number. Do the other side too, because the gap between sides is part of the story. If one hip pinches at the front while the other swings free, you just found the hip that has been quietly limiting every squat you own. Keep your number. At the end of this video I will tell you exactly what it means.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN PINCH AND FREE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty five degrees of clean internal rotation is where a hip stops pinching and starts turning freely. Under twenty, the joint runs out of turn early, and something else has to absorb every deep position you force it into. That something is usually the tissue at the front of the hip, and it complains exactly the way you have been feeling. Between twenty and thirty five, the hip is building: the turn exists, it just needs training. Over forty, your hip owns the full gear. Most skinny guys test lower than they expect, not because the joint is broken, but because nothing in modern life ever asks the hip to rotate.
scenes.sub: under 20: stiff and pinching - over 40: full rotation

scenes.narration: Look at the shape of this joint. The hip is a ball sitting deep inside a socket, wrapped in a capsule of tough tissue and a team of small rotator muscles buried under the big ones. Rotation is the movement that lets the ball spin inside the socket without hitting the walls. When rotation runs out early, deep positions do not stop politely. The ball rolls forward, the front of the socket gets crowded, and the soft tissue there gets pinched between bone and bone. That pinch is not damage happening in real time. It is a traffic jam. The tissue at the front of your hip is being compressed because the turn that should have made room never arrived. Healing, for this tissue, does not mean stretching it harder. It means restoring the turn, so the compression stops happening in the first place.

Here is what almost nobody tells you about rotation. Every big movement you love borrows it. A deep squat needs the hip to rotate as it folds. A kick needs it. Changing direction at speed needs it most of all. When the turn is missing, the body does not cancel the movement. It steals the motion from somewhere else, usually the lower back, and it pays the front of the hip as the toll. Clinicians who measure hips for a living see the same pattern again and again: the sore, pinching side almost always turns less than the quiet side. That gap is the most useful number in this whole video, because a gap can be closed. Tissue remodels toward the loads you repeat. Give the hip thousands of small, pain-free turns in the middle of its range, and the capsule and rotators gradually reorganize around the new capacity. That is not a stretch. That is construction.

Now the mistake almost everyone makes, and the title of this video. When a hip pinches, people stretch it by forcing it deeper into the exact position that pinches: deeper squats, harder pigeon stretches, knees pushed wider under load. Every rep squeezes the irritated tissue again and calls it treatment. Compression is the one language this tissue cannot heal from. What it heals from is tension in safe ranges: the deep rotators working hard while the joint sits in the middle of its range, nowhere near the pinch. Think of it like a sprained ankle. You would never heal it by standing on it twisted. You heal it by loading it straight, gently, often. The hip is the same deal, just buried deeper and complaining in a stranger accent.

Here is the part where being skinny quietly wins. The pinch gets worse with load at end range, and a heavy body brings a lot of load to every deep position whether it wants to or not. Your bodyweight is smaller, which means your daily rotation work costs the joint less, and you can repeat it more often without paying for it tomorrow. Frequency is the whole game with tissue remodeling. Ten calm turns every day will rebuild a hip faster than one heroic stretching session a week that leaves the front of the joint angry for three days. You also recover faster between sessions for the same reason: less total load to clear. The big guy has to schedule his hip work around his squats. You can hide yours inside a normal Tuesday, between the chair and the kitchen, and the tissue will never know it was ambushed.

Train with me. Sit tall, shin out to your comfortable stop, then press the shin outward into your hand while your hand refuses to move. Hard press, zero movement. Thirty seconds a side. This is rotation strength with no pinch invited.

Here is your week. Every day, the rotation presses you just did, four rounds a side, always stopping the swing before the pinch speaks. Three days a week, add slow squats to the deepest depth that stays completely pinch-free, even if that depth is embarrassingly high at first. That depth is not a failure. It is the border of the construction zone, and it moves. Walk on the other days, because hips love rhythm. Now the mistakes to retire. Forcing the pigeon stretch through the pinch: retired. Cracking the hip loose before training: retired. Training only the good side because it feels better: retired, the gap is the target. And the rule that outranks every drill in this video: if the pinch is sharp, if the hip clicks with pain, or if it keeps getting worse week after week, see a professional if it persists. Joints that lock or give way deserve eyes, not videos.

So, your number. Under twenty degrees: your hip is guarded, not broken, and it needs weeks of mid-range turns before depth work means anything. Twenty to thirty five: you are building, the turn is coming back, and the pinch should visit less often as the gap closes. Over thirty five: your hip owns its rotation, and any pinch left is a load problem, not a mobility problem. Write your degrees in the comments, both sides, just the numbers. In thirty days we run the wiper again and compare. Hips do not heal by being forced. They heal by being taught to turn.

Your hip already knows how to turn. It just stopped being asked. Ask it gently, ask it daily, and in thirty days we measure the answer together. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing hip pinch Wrong: Train Your hip tissue healing Instead
